unit: One engine coolant temperature sensor, fitted. Some engines have two (one on the engine and one at the radiator or thermostat housing); this is the price for one. Not included: diagnosis of the warning light, gauge reading or code, coolant to top up what is lost when the sensor comes out, a coolant drain and refill or air bleed, the thermostat or its housing, and wiring or connector repair.

finding: The site has no live range for this job, so there is nothing to grade; these are first figures and they are weak on labor. Built totals (part + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks), for one sensor: economy 2014 Dodge Dart about $107-$228; midsize 2014 Jeep Grand Cherokee 3.6L about $102-$228; truck 2014 Ram 1500 3.6L about $82-$228; large near-luxury 2014 Chrysler 300 3.6L about $102-$221. A supportable range for an easy-to-reach sensor is therefore roughly $80-$230. Against the benchmarks: the built totals sit at the low end of YourMechanic's RAV4 table ($135-$434) and TorqueMech ($120-$450+) and far below RepairPal ($499-$585). The gap to RepairPal is mostly parts: it prices parts at $343-$356 while the genuine sensors verified here list at $60.55-$67.60, so RepairPal's figure looks weighted toward vehicles where the sensor is sold with a housing or other parts. Treat the built totals as the low side of what a shop will quote. How solid the labor times are, stated plainly: weak, which is why confidence is low. No maker-stated time for replacing only this sensor, printed with a unit and free of diagnosis or inspection, was found for any class. All four classes use one general statement by a named diagnostic technician, 30 to 60 minutes, which is not a flat-rate book time and not for the example vehicles; the truck low end is a parts seller's approximate 20-minute do-it-yourself figure for the Ram 1500 3.6L. The maker times found all carry something extra and are cross-checks only: FCA allows 1.0 Hrs. to inspect and replace the sensor on the 2023 Grand Cherokee 3.6L (0.2 Hrs. to inspect only); Mazda allows 0.7 Hrs. on the 2014-2017 Mazda3 for the second sensor at the radiator, with a scan-tool comparison included; Hyundai prints 0.8 with no unit on the 2021-2022 Elantra, which includes sanding the mounting hole; MINI prints 4 FRU, a BMW time unit not converted here. A parts retailer's guide by a named author gives 45 minutes on the 1.8T Volkswagen and Audi. Together these point to roughly half an hour to one hour, so the range used is consistent with them, but none can carry a range end. General Motors, Honda and Acura, Nissan, Subaru and Ford bulletins with a coolant temperature sensor time were searched for and none was found. Limits: no stated time was found for an engine where the sensor is buried (under an intake manifold or behind other parts), and a job that needs the cooling system drained, refilled and bled will cost more than these totals. Parts: every class has a genuine list price from a dealer catalog page for the example vehicle and year. No aftermarket price on a page that said new was found, so each low end is the genuine sensor at a dealer's discounted online price ($42.35-$47.24); aftermarket sensors were seen at $13.49, $18.99 and $29.69 on pages that did not state condition, so a shop using one could come in lower on parts. The 3.6L V6 has two sensors in the catalog ($60.55 and $67.60) and the range covers either. The luxury class is the weakest fit: the example is a near-luxury sedan, not a luxury-brand car, because no luxury-brand part price was loaded. An estimate is not a quote and not a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds a diagnosis fee, coolant to top up or a full drain, refill and air bleed (some coolant is lost when the sensor comes out), a new sealing washer, O-ring or retaining clip, shop supplies and sales tax. A thermostat or thermostat housing is often quoted at the same time, and on some engines the sensor is only sold as part of the housing, which raises the parts price. Wiring or connector repair is separate, as is the second sensor on engines that have two.
held_reason: Held at review after one attempt: every labor range rests on one general guide (30 to 60 minutes), no maker prints a sensor-only time with a unit, every low is the genuine part discounted, and the luxury example (Chrysler 300) is not a luxury make.
